title: Power Query: import & transform
goal: Load a CSV with Power Query, understand the cleaning steps it records, spot the data-type trap, and refresh next month's file in one go.

steps.text:
Every month the bank emails the same messy CSV. Cleaning it with formulas means **redoing every fix, every month**.

**Power Query** is Excel's built-in cleaning robot. You clean the file **once**, and it writes down each action as a list called **Applied Steps** (shown below). Next month you click **Refresh** and it replays the whole list on the new file.

The journey has three parts:
• **Load**: on the **Data** tab, choose **Get Data → From File → From Text/CSV** and pick the file.
• **Clean**: click **Transform Data** to open the Power Query Editor. Remove columns, set data types, split, trim. Each action adds a line to Applied Steps.
• **Close & Load**: the clean table lands in your sheet.

The editor can't run inside this lesson, so you'll practise by working out what each step would produce.

steps.prompt:
A new `sales_aug.csv` arrives and you want a **repeatable** clean-up.

Which order is right?
options: Get Data → clean in the editor → Close & Load
Close & Load → fix the sheet by hand → Get Data
Clean the CSV in Excel → then Get Data
steps.explain: **Get Data → Transform Data → Close & Load** records every action as a step. If you fix the data by hand before or after loading, nothing is recorded, and next month you start from zero.
wrongFeedback: Hand edits on the loaded sheet are never recorded, and a refresh will overwrite them.
That cleans this month once, but Power Query has recorded nothing to replay next month.
clues: Where does Power Query write the steps down? Inside the editor.

steps.prompt:
You opened the file in the editor. The bank adds an **Internal code** you never use.

Click the header of the column you'd remove (in the editor: right-click it → **Remove Columns**), then press [[Enter]].
steps.wrongFeedback: That column is useful. The one to drop is **Internal code**: click its letter, `D`.
clues: Which column would nobody in your team read?

steps.prompt:
**Split Column → By Delimiter** cuts one column into several at a divider. Splitting `TEE-BLUE-L` at every `-` gives three columns: `TEE`, `BLUE`, `L`.

In ==B3==, work out what the **middle** column will hold for the second row. Take everything after the first dash, then everything before the next one.
steps.explain: **BLUE**. `TEXTAFTER(A3,"-")` leaves `BLUE-L`, then `TEXTBEFORE(...,"-")` keeps `BLUE`. Power Query does this with one click and remembers it as a **Split Column** step.

wrongFeedback.wrongValue: You want only the middle piece. After the first dash you still have `BLUE-L`: cut again at the next dash.

clues: `=TEXTAFTER(A3,"-")` gives `BLUE-L`. Wrap it in TEXTBEFORE with the same dash.

steps.prompt:
Power Query guesses each column's **data type** from its first rows, and adds a **Changed Type** step. Usually that's a help. Here it's a trap.

The IDs `00417`, `00532` look like numbers, so Power Query picks **Whole Number**. In ==B2==, show what the first ID becomes.
steps.explain: **417**: the leading zeros are gone. A number has no “leading zeros”, so `00417` quietly becomes `417`. Always scan the **Changed Type** step for IDs, phone numbers and postcodes.

wrongFeedback.missingFunction: Use **VALUE** to turn the text into a number, like Whole Number does.
wrongFeedback.wrongValue: A whole number drops the zeros. Try `=VALUE(A2)`.

steps.prompt:
The loaded table now shows `417`, but your shipping labels need `00417`.

What's the best fix?
options: Set the column's type to **Text** in the editor
Retype the zeros on the sheet
steps.explain: Changing the type to **Text** is itself a recorded step, so next month's refresh keeps the zeros too. Fixing it on the sheet is wiped by the next refresh.
wrongFeedback: Edits on the loaded sheet are overwritten when you refresh, and you'd redo them every month.
That only changes how the number looks. The ID is still a number, so a lookup against text IDs elsewhere would fail.
clues: Fix it where the steps are recorded.

steps.prompt:
The ▾ on a column header in the editor works like a filter, and adds a **Filtered Rows** step. You keep **only Paid** rows.

In ==B8==, work out what the **Amount** column of the loaded table adds up to.
steps.explain: **4350** = 1250 + 2300 + 800. Rahul, Neha and Kabir are filtered out of the table. The same filter runs again on next month's file, whatever it contains.

wrongFeedback.missingFunction: Add up only the rows that match **Paid**.
wrongFeedback.wrongValue: Only the three Paid rows: 1250, 2300 and 800. A plain SUM of the column gives 5700.

clues: Condition column is `C2:C7`, the numbers to add are `B2:B7`.

steps.prompt:
Next month the bank sends a new file with **5 more orders** and the same messy habits. You save it over the old file (same name, same folder) and click **Refresh**.

What will the loaded table do?
options: Add the 5 new rows, already cleaned
Add the 5 new rows, still messy
steps.explain: Refresh re-reads the file and replays every Applied Step on **all** of it, so the new rows come out trimmed, typed and filtered like the old ones. Keep the file name and column headings the same, or the steps can't find their columns.
wrongFeedback: The steps are the whole point: they run on every row in the file, new ones included.
The query is a live link to the file, not a one-time copy, so a refresh pulls in what changed.
clues: What did the Applied Steps list do for you the first time?

steps.prompt:
The new file is saved. Your query table is selected.

Press [[Ctrl]] + [[Alt]] + [[F5]] to **Refresh All**. It's the same as **Data → Refresh All**, and it refreshes every query in the workbook.

On a Mac, use **Data → Refresh All**.
clues: Hold Ctrl and Alt together, then tap F5.

steps.prompt:
In the loaded table you spot the typo **Rahul Metha** and fix it directly in the cell. Next month you click Refresh.

What happens to your fix?
steps.explain: The loaded table is **output**: refresh rebuilds it from the file and the steps. To fix a typo for good, correct the source file or add a **Replace Values** step in the editor.
wrongFeedback: Only the steps persist. Refresh redraws the table from scratch.
Excel refreshes happily and silently overwrites your edit, which is why this mistake is so common.
clues: Is the table the source of the data, or the result?

steps.prompt:
This month's file lists some orders twice. The query ends with a **Remove Duplicates** step on the Order column.

In ==D2==, how many rows will the loaded table have?
steps.explain: **5**: R50 to R54. The seven rows contain R50 and R51 twice, and Remove Duplicates keeps the first of each. In the editor it's one click, and it's re-applied on every refresh.

wrongFeedback.wrongValue: Count each Order **once**. Seven rows, but how many different order numbers?

clues: Count the different Order numbers, not the rows.
`UNIQUE` lists each value once, and `ROWS` counts them.
